item.title: How crypto loans unwind: what a $43.8 million ether sale teaches about leverage
item.description:
BTCS's sale is too small to move ether's price directly. The bigger effect is on how investors view listed crypto treasury firms, whose shares tend to trade as leveraged bets on the coins they hold. BTCS fell nearly 9%. The episode may push investors to look harder at how much other ether-heavy companies have borrowed. Spot ether ETFs are in a run of outflows and bitcoin is below $60,000, so risk appetite across crypto is fragile. Further forced-sale disclosures could hurt sentiment more than they add to supply.

-

A balance sheet that looked well covered on paper was only a 19% ether drop from forced liquidation, and BTCS paid to close that gap before Aave closed it for them.

Summary:

  • BTCS sold about 27,300 ETH on November 20 for $43.8 million and used it all to repay Aave debt, per an 8-K filed November 23.
  • Its Aave borrowing fell to about $10.5 million from an implied $54.3 million.
  • Its November 9 position (about $64.1 million owed against 46,676 ETH) implied a liquidation price of around $1,720. Ether fell near $1,560 on November 20.
  • The company is left with about 24,245 ETH. TheStreet puts its loan-to-value ratio at about 32%.
  • Its DeFi unit, Imperium, has paused its liquidity pool positions, and about $17.9 million of convertible notes are due in 2027.

Nasdaq-listed BTCS sold about 27,300 ETH on November 20 and used the full $43.8 million in proceeds to repay debt on Aave, the decentralised lending protocol, according to a Form 8-K filed with the SEC on November 23. The sale cut its Aave borrowing to roughly $10.5 million. It came as ether briefly fell near $1,560, below a liquidation level that had been estimated from the company's own quarterly filing only days earlier.

The deal is small for the ether market. But it is a clear, documented example of how crypto-backed borrowing works, and of how quickly a comfortable-looking position can become a forced sale.

How an Aave loan works

Aave lends stablecoins against crypto collateral, and every loan is overcollateralised: the borrower must lock up more value than it borrows. Three measures matter.

Loan-to-value (LTV) is the debt divided by the value of the collateral. A $50 loan against $100 of ether is a 50% LTV.

The liquidation threshold is the share of collateral value Aave will count when judging whether a loan is safe. BTCS has said this is generally 80% for ETH.

The health factor combines the two: collateral value multiplied by the liquidation threshold, divided by the debt. Above 1, the loan is safe. Below 1, Aave's smart contracts can sell the borrower's collateral automatically to repay the lender, with no phone call and no negotiation.

The BTCS numbers, worked through

BTCS's quarterly filing showed it owed about $64.1 million on Aave as of November 9. That was backed by 46,676 ETH valued at about $99.3 million, using an ether price of around $2,130. The collateral covered the debt about 1.55 times over, which sounds like a wide margin.

Apply the 80% threshold, though, and the health factor comes out near 1.24. That implies a liquidation price of around $1,720 per ETH, close to CoinDesk's own estimate. In other words, collateral worth 155% of the debt left a price buffer of only about 19%.

Ether then fell roughly 27% from the $2,130 marker to its November 20 low. BTCS had already cut its debt to an implied $54.3 million before that day, which would have lowered its real liquidation line. The company has not disclosed where that line sat. What the filings do show is that it chose to sell rather than wait.

Why sell before the protocol does

A borrower facing a falling health factor has three choices: add collateral, repay debt, or let the protocol liquidate. BTCS held very little cash, reporting about $463,000 at the end of September, so adding collateral meant finding ether it did not have. Liquidation would have meant selling on the protocol's terms, at the worst moment and with a penalty attached.

Selling its own ether to repay the debt let BTCS choose the timing. Chief executive Charles Allen said, according to TheStreet, that the company preferred to cut its Aave borrowing rather than carry the debt through a falling market. The cost is permanent. The average sale price, around $1,600, locks in the loss, and BTCS is left with about 24,245 ETH. "We are a smaller company today," Allen said.

What the sale did to the risk

TheStreet reported the company's loan-to-value ratio at about 32% after the repayment. On that figure, and using the same 80% threshold, ether would need to fall about 60% before the remaining loan neared liquidation. That works out to roughly $690, based on the $1,722 price BTCS used for November 22. This is an illustration rather than a disclosed level, but it shows how much room paying down debt buys.

The trade-off is that the company now has less ether to earn from. Its DeFi unit, Imperium, has temporarily exited its liquidity pool positions. BTCS also still has about $17.9 million of senior secured convertible notes due in May and July 2027. Its shares fell nearly 9%.

Does one forced seller move ether?

Not on its own. The $43.8 million sale is roughly a quarter of 1% of the $17 billion or so in ether traded over 24 hours, according to CoinGecko data. The more useful signal for ETH holders is the pattern. Companies and traders who borrow against ether all face the same arithmetic, and a falling price can push several of them to sell at once. That is how leverage can turn a decline into a sharper one, even when no single seller is large.

The backdrop is already weak. Ether traded around $1,690 on Wednesday in Asia, down roughly 28% over the past month, after a bounce to around $1,840 on November 23 failed to hold. US spot ether ETFs recorded a seventh straight day of net outflows on November 23, according to SoSoValue data, and bitcoin dropped below $60,000 for the first time since July.

What to watch next

The next thing to watch is further disclosure. Another BTCS 8-K showing more sales, or new borrowing, would show whether this was a one-off reset or the start of a longer unwind. The same goes for other listed companies holding ether on borrowed money. Their filings will show how close their collateral sits to the 80% line.

ETF flows are the second marker. A return to inflows while ether holds above its November 20 low would suggest forced selling is easing. Continued outflows alongside new lows would raise the odds that more leveraged holders face the choice BTCS faced.

What could change the reading: if ether recovers quickly, BTCS's sale will look like expensive insurance it never needed. That would not make it the wrong call. A health factor measures how far the price can fall before someone else decides for you, and the cheapest time to act is before that room runs out.

Key terms:

Overcollateralised: a loan backed by collateral worth more than the amount borrowed.

Liquidation threshold: the share of collateral value a lending protocol counts toward a loan's safety.

Health factor: collateral value multiplied by the liquidation threshold, divided by the debt. Below 1, the collateral can be sold automatically.

Form 8-K: a US filing companies use to report major events between quarterly reports.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Saudi Arabia triples its oil storage in Japan as Tokyo buys 8m barrels to refill reserves
item.description:
Japan's purchase of up to 8 million barrels is modest against global flows, but it adds a source of committed demand just as oil sells off on surplus fears. Restocking by consumers whose emergency reserves were drawn down this year could put a floor under prompt crude demand. For Saudi Arabia, extra storage in Japan gives it barrels positioned close to Asian buyers, which helps it respond quickly to disruptions and defend market share as Gulf flows recover. If other importers strike similar arrangements, as MUFG expects, the trend would support Middle Eastern exporters' long-term grip on Asian demand.

--

Japan is restocking its emergency reserves with Saudi crude and giving Riyadh three times more room to store oil on Japanese soil, a sign that this year's Gulf disruptions are pushing buyers and sellers toward deeper supply partnerships.

Summary:

  • Japan will buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to refill its strategic petroleum reserve
  • Saudi Arabia gains access to a further 16 million barrels of storage in Japan, on top of 8 million already available
  • Saudi Arabia supplied 42% of Japan's crude imports in 2025, with the UAE close behind at 41%
  • The Middle East accounted for 93% of Japan's total oil imports
  • The deal secures supply for Japan and a reliable outlet for Saudi exports
  • MUFG expects more storage deals and wider access for Gulf exporters after this year's disruptions

Japan and Saudi Arabia have agreed a strategic oil storage arrangement that will see Tokyo buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to refill its petroleum reserve, while Riyadh gains significantly more space to store oil on Japanese soil. Under the deal, Saudi Arabia will have access to a further 16 million barrels of storage capacity in Japan, adding to the 8 million barrels it already had and tripling its total to 24 million barrels, according to a note from MUFG.

The agreement reflects Japan's heavy dependence on Gulf supply. Saudi Arabia was Japan's largest source of crude imports in 2025, accounting for 42% of the total, with the United Arab Emirates close behind at 41%. Overall, oil from the Middle East made up 93% of Japan's imports, leaving the country among the most exposed of the major consumers to disruption in the region.

That exposure has been tested this year, as conflict in the Middle East disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and pushed consumer nations to draw on emergency stocks. Refilling those reserves is now a priority for importers, and long-term supply relationships offer a way to rebuild them with greater certainty.

The benefits run both ways. For Japan, a larger and more durable link with its biggest supplier helps secure access to crude in a crisis. For Saudi Arabia, storage in Japan provides a reliable destination for its exports and positions barrels close to major Asian buyers, allowing quicker deliveries when supply chains are strained elsewhere.

MUFG expects the model to spread. It sees scope for existing storage facilities to be expanded, and for Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern exporters to secure storage access in a wider range of countries, as both producers and consumers look to guard against a repeat of this year's disruption. With oil prices under pressure from expectations of a looming surplus, such arrangements could also help Gulf exporters lock in demand as their shipments recover. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump floats a US government stake in Nvidia, calling the chipmaker vital to AI leadership
item.description:
The prospect of federal ownership adds a new policy variable to the most important stock in the AI trade, at a time when sentiment toward the sector is already fragile. Investors could read open White House backing as a floor under Nvidia's strategic position. They could also read it as a source of governance risk and political entanglement, especially on export rules and China sales. Any move would also be watched closely by global chip peers and by governments elsewhere weighing similar steps. With Huang testifying next week, headline risk around Nvidia, and through it the wider semiconductor and Nasdaq complex, is likely to stay elevated.

-

Trump's offer to pardon Jensen Huang grabbed attention, but his openness to Washington taking a stake in Nvidia is the more consequential signal for the AI trade and the reach of US industrial policy.

Summary:

  • Trump said he has considered a US government equity stake in Nvidia but has not yet raised it, adding it may not be too late
  • He described Nvidia's success as crucial to US leadership in artificial intelligence
  • Trump said he would pardon CEO Jensen Huang if necessary, but expects Huang to be fine without one
  • Huang testifies before Congress next week, and Trump said he should tell the truth and need not invoke the Fifth Amendment
  • Trump had pressed Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang, sparking a sharp rally in the shares on Monday
  • The stock slipped on Tuesday but recovered much of the loss by the close

President Donald Trump has opened the door to the US government taking an equity stake in Nvidia, describing the chipmaker's success as central to keeping the United States ahead in artificial intelligence. In an interview with the New York Post, Trump said he had thought about the idea but had not yet raised it, adding that it might not be too late to do so.

The comments came alongside a more personal show of support for Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, who is due to testify before Congress next week. Trump said he would be willing to pardon Huang if it became necessary, though he expected Huang to be fine without one, and said Huang should simply tell the truth to lawmakers and would have no need to invoke his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. Trump had earlier pressed Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang, a move that sparked a sharp rally in the shares on Monday. Reviewing market data from the Oval Office, he noted that the stock had slipped on Tuesday but recovered much of the ground by the close.

The stake remark is the more significant for markets. Washington has already shown a willingness to take equity in strategically important companies, most notably its stake in Intel in 2025, as part of a broader push to secure domestic capacity in semiconductors and critical supply chains. Extending that approach to Nvidia, the dominant supplier of the chips that power AI data centres and one of the world's most valuable companies, would mark a significant step up in state involvement in the sector.

No proposal has been made, and Trump stressed that he had not yet raised it with the company. The structure, size and purpose of any stake remain entirely open, as does the question of how Nvidia's board and shareholders would respond.

For investors, the remarks underline how closely the fortunes of the AI trade are now tied to policy in Washington. Government backing could be read as support for Nvidia's strategic position, but it also raises questions about governance, export policy and the company's independence. Huang's testimony next week and any follow-up from the White House are likely to be the next markers. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Barclays holds $100 Brent call for 2026, says bearish oil positioning ignores tight supply
item.description:
Barclays' note gives oil bulls a fundamental case just as speculative length sits near extreme lows. That makes crude vulnerable to sharp short-covering rallies on any Hormuz incident, a stalled diplomatic track or an OPEC+ surprise on Sunday. Brent calendar spreads are the clearest signal to watch: firmness in nearby contracts would support the bank's physical tightness argument even if flat prices stay heavy. For now, oil is trading as a risk asset alongside equities and copper, so a turn in broader sentiment could matter as much as any Gulf headline. Any rebound would be a renewed headache for central banks fighting energy-driven inflation. Though a faster-than-expected recovery in Gulf exports would undercut the bank's case.

Barclays argues that oil is being sold for the wrong reasons, with traders reacting to risk-off moves elsewhere while Gulf flows, inventories and Asian demand still point to a tighter market than prices suggest.

Summary:

  • Barclays sees no fundamental justification for extremely depressed speculative positioning in oil
  • Recent selling reflects cross-asset risk aversion and Fed hike expectations rather than easing Middle East tension
  • Light positioning and cheap upside options leave room for a sharp short-covering rally
  • Middle East exports are at about 85% of pre-war levels, ex-China inventories are low and strategic reserve releases have mostly ended
  • Demand from China and India continues to recover
  • Brent forecasts are held at $100 for 2026 and $85 for 2027, with a long Brent calendar spread recommendation

Barclays is pushing back against the latest leg of the oil sell-off, arguing that speculative positioning in crude futures has become far more bearish than physical supply or geopolitics can justify. With Brent trading below $90 a barrel, the bank said in its latest commodity research note that it sees no common thread to explain such depressed positioning and that risks to prices remain skewed higher. It kept its Brent forecasts at $100 a barrel for 2026 and $85 for 2027.

The bank's central point is that the reason for selling has changed. Earlier declines were driven by hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough between Washington and Tehran, optimism Barclays had already judged premature. The more recent pressure, it argues, has come from broad cross-asset risk aversion, including weaker equities, growth worries and expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening, rather than any genuine easing of tension in the Middle East.

That leaves the market lopsided. Speculative long positions in oil futures are near extreme lows and options markets are not pricing much risk of a price spike. In Barclays' view, that combination means even a modest supply disruption or a turn in macro sentiment could force traders to cover short positions quickly, driving a sharp move higher.

The physical picture supports that case, according to the bank. Export flows from the Middle East are running at roughly 85% of pre-war levels on a 30-day average, as disruption around the Strait of Hormuz continues. Oil inventories outside China remain well below historical norms, and most of the emergency releases from strategic reserves have now wound down, removing a source of supply that cushioned the market earlier in the year. Demand from major Asian buyers, including China and India, continues to recover.

The bank's view runs against a growing body of opinion that the market is heading into surplus. The International Energy Agency expects the global oil balance to swing back to surplus in the fourth quarter for the first time since the war began, as Middle Eastern exports recover faster than demand. JPMorgan has warned that once the conflict eases, Gulf producers outside Iran could move quickly to win back lost market share, while the reopening of Libya's Sharara pipeline has added to near-term supply.

Barclays' counter is that recovering flows are still well short of pre-war levels and that inventories remain too thin to absorb a fresh disruption. Which view prevails is likely to depend on the direction of US-Iran talks, the decisions OPEC+ takes at its meeting on Sunday, and whether the wider risk-off mood across equities and commodities begins to fade. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US PCE preview: inflation seen near 3.8% in the Fed's last read before a December hike
item.description:
With a December hike largely priced, the reaction is more likely to come through expectations for early 2027. A core print of 0.4% or more would probably lift front-end Treasury yields and the dollar as traders add to bets on follow-up hikes in January or March. A 0.2% reading would ease that pressure without removing the December move. Gold is exposed to a hot print, since higher rate expectations have weighed on it throughout this tightening cycle. Thin Thanksgiving liquidity adds to the risk of outsized moves across FX, bonds and equity futures.

---

A December Fed hike looks all but settled, so Wednesday's October PCE report is really about what comes next, with a firm core reading likely to strengthen the case for further tightening early in 2027.

Summary:

  • October PCE is due 13:30 GMT (8:30am US Eastern) Wednesday, the last major inflation read before the 9 December Fed decision
  • Headline PCE is expected near 3.8% y/y from 3.6%, and core around 3.2% from 3.1%
  • Monthly core forecasts cluster near 0.3%, with some as high as 0.4%
  • It is the only annual inflation rate for October, as October CPI was published without one
  • Markets price about a 90% chance of a 25bp December hike from the current 3.75% to 4.00% range
  • Q3 GDP, jobless claims and income and spending data land at the same time, with the Beige Book at 19:00 GMT

The US October personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, due at 13:30 GMT (8:30am US Eastern) on Wednesday, is the last major inflation reading the Federal Reserve will see before its 9 December decision, and it arrives with a rate hike already largely priced. The question for markets is less whether the Fed tightens in December than how far it goes after that. Headline PCE inflation is expected to rise to around 3.8% year on year from 3.6% in September, in line with the Cleveland Fed's inflation nowcast, while core PCE, which strips out food and energy and is the Fed's preferred gauge, is seen edging up to around 3.2% from 3.1%.

The monthly core number is likely to drive the reaction. Most forecasts sit near 0.3%, with Goldman Sachs at 0.3% after trimming its estimate, and some research houses as high as 0.4%. Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said earlier this month that progress on inflation appeared to have stalled and that she expected annual core PCE of around 3.3% for October.

This report carries extra weight because October's consumer price index was published without an annual rate. Price collection was disrupted during the 2025 government shutdown, leaving no year-ago base, so PCE provides the only year-on-year inflation measure for October. That CPI report showed monthly gains of 0.4% for the headline and 0.3% for core, both a tenth above forecasts, while producer prices have been running at their fastest annual pace since late 2022.

The Fed raised rates in September to a 3.75% to 4.00% target range and held in October in a 10 to 2 vote, with two dissenters preferring a hike. Futures put the odds of a quarter-point increase in December at around 90%. Goldman Sachs expects hikes in December and March, while Bank of America sees three quarter-point increases in December, January and March, so a firm core reading would mainly feed into expectations for the early months of 2027.

Several other releases land at the same time, including the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, weekly jobless claims brought forward because of Thanksgiving, and personal income and spending. The Fed's Beige Book follows at 19:00 GMT. With US equity markets closed on Thursday and closing early on Friday, thin holiday liquidity could amplify any surprise.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Deutsche Bank sees S&P 500 at 9,000 by end-2027, 25% upside on AI-driven earnings
item.description:
A 9,000 target from a major bank, alongside a warning that the current sell-off may not have bottomed, gives dip buyers a reason to hold on while leaving room for further near-term losses. AI-linked megacaps and capex beneficiaries stand to gain most if the productivity case holds, but they would also feel the overinvestment risk first. The fiscal warning matters for bonds: heavier government borrowing points to more Treasury supply, which could keep long-end yields elevated and cap equity valuations. European equities get a valuation-based endorsement, with the Stoxx 600 seen as cheap relative to its recent range.

---

Deutsche Bank is betting that AI-driven earnings will carry the S&P 500 to 9,000 by end-2027, though its own strategists warn the route will be anything but smooth.

Summary:

  • Deutsche Bank targets 9,000 for the S&P 500 at end-2027, about 25% above current levels
  • Its demand and supply model puts equities around 20% below the level implied by 2027 earnings
  • The bank sees AI capex already lifting US growth and early productivity gains in AI-heavy sectors
  • The Stoxx 600 is forecast at 750, roughly 20% upside, with forward valuations near the low end of their range
  • It sees the recent sell-off as a volatility event that may deepen before bottoming
  • The risks it flags are AI overinvestment, fiscal expansion adding to debt and bond supply, and defence and energy spending raising geopolitical tension

Deutsche Bank expects the S&P 500 to reach 9,000 by the end of 2027, about 25% above current levels, putting the bank at the bullish end of Wall Street's year-ahead forecasts. The call, from the bank's equity strategists and reported by Seeking Alpha, rests on what they describe as a very supportive earnings outlook and a conviction that artificial intelligence will lift productivity across the economy.

The target sits well above JPMorgan's 8,200 and above the 8,700 forecasts from Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, making Deutsche Bank one of the most optimistic of the major houses so far in outlook season.

Jim Reid, the bank's global head of macro and thematic research, characterised recent market turbulence as a volatility event that may run further before it bottoms out but is unlikely to undermine the fundamentals. He argued that AI-related capital spending is already large enough to move US growth, and that early evidence points to faster productivity gains in the sectors that use AI most intensively.

The forecast is built on Deutsche Bank's demand and supply framework for equities, which suggests prices are currently around 20% below the level implied by projected year-end 2027 earnings on historical relationships. In Europe, the strategists see the Stoxx 600 climbing to 750, roughly 20% upside, noting that forward valuations sit near the bottom of their recent range.

Reid was careful to temper the optimism. He noted that technology revolutions driven by heavy investment have historically been uneven, with overinvestment, busts and surprise winners and losers along the way. The capital needed to deliver an AI productivity breakthrough could itself lead to excess. He also flagged government spending, which may support growth but adds to bond supply and debt, and the push for strategic autonomy, which demands heavy outlays on defence, energy and technology while raising geopolitical tension.

His conclusion was that 2027 could turn out to be a very good year for investors if expectations are met, but that it is unlikely to feel that way on a day-to-day basis. For markets still digesting an AI-led sell-off and a Federal Reserve on a hiking path, the gap between Deutsche Bank's 9,000 and more cautious calls near 8,200 shows how widely views differ on whether earnings can outrun tighter policy. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: JPMorgan's 8,200 S&P 500 target for 2027 sits below peers as Fed risk tempers AI upside
item.description:
A major bank calling the recent tech sell-off a better entry point could support dip buying in AI-linked megacaps, though the below-consensus target also argues for keeping expectations in check. Rate-sensitive sectors look most exposed to the risk JPMorgan names, and so do richly valued growth names, if Fed tightening pushes financial conditions tighter still. For futures traders, the note adds to a two-sided view: positioning has reset, but sentiment is fragile and liquidity thinner, which could keep volatility high through year-end.

---

JPMorgan still sees AI earnings lifting US stocks through 2027, but its 8,200 target leaves less room than rival banks' targets do for a Fed that stays tight.

Summary:

  • JPMorgan targets 8,200 for the S&P 500 at end-2027, about 14% upside
  • The target is below the Bloomberg consensus near 8,470 and the 8,700 calls from Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley
  • The bank expects above-trend earnings growth from an AI investment cycle it sees as broadly intact
  • It says the recent momentum unwind and positioning reset improved near-term risk-reward
  • The S&P 500 is about 8% below its October record after an AI-led sell-off
  • The main risk is damage from Fed tightening amid weaker liquidity and fragile sentiment

JPMorgan expects the S&P 500 to end 2027 at 8,200, a gain of about 14% from current levels, but its target sits at the cautious end of Wall Street forecasts as rising US interest rates cloud the outlook. The call, from the bank's global markets strategy team led by Dubravko Lakos-Bujas, is below a consensus of around 8,470 compiled by Bloomberg, and well short of the 8,700 year-end targets set by strategists at Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. It is in line with forecasts from UBS Global Wealth Management, Wells Fargo and Bank of America.

The strategists remain constructive on the earnings picture. They expect above-trend profit growth tied to what they describe as an AI supercycle, arguing that demand for computing power and the rapid pace of technical progress should support another year of heavy AI investment. In their view, the AI cycle is broadly intact despite recent doubts over the pace and financing of that spending.

They also see an opportunity in the recent sell-off. A momentum unwind and a broader reset in positioning have, the team argues, improved the near-term risk-reward for equities. The S&P 500 is up nearly 5% this year but roughly 8% below its October record near 7,840, with AI-linked stocks leading the decline.

The restraint in the target comes from the policy backdrop. Higher interest rates and uncertainty around AI following the US midterm elections have weighed on sentiment, and the strategists see a gradual recovery only if the Federal Reserve gives more weight to its growth mandate alongside price stability. The main risk they identify is collateral damage from monetary tightening, at a time when financial conditions and liquidity have already worsened and investor sentiment remains fragile.

That framing puts the Fed at the centre of the 2027 equity story. With the central bank on a hiking path, one reading of JPMorgan's call is that earnings can still carry US stocks higher, but with less help from rising valuations than its more bullish peers may be counting on. The gap between the 8,200 and 8,700 camps is likely to narrow or widen depending on how quickly inflation eases and whether the Fed signals that its tightening is close to an end. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Private survey shows US crude stocks barely rising, well short of the 0.9 million barrel forecast
item.description:
A smaller-than-expected crude build and a draw at Cushing lean modestly supportive for WTI, particularly for nearby contracts, after a month in which prices have fallen sharply. The flat gasoline figure against an expected build points to steady pre-holiday fuel demand. The effect is likely to be limited unless Wednesday's official numbers confirm it. Supply headlines carry more weight for now: the risk to Hormuz shipping, progress in US-Iran talks and Sunday's OPEC+ meeting will probably set the tone for both benchmarks. Thinner trade around Thanksgiving could exaggerate any move.

Private industry data shows US crude stocks barely rising and Cushing drawing down, offering a small counterweight to the supply glut worries that have pushed oil toward three-month lows.

Summary:

  • Crude stocks rose about 0.1 million barrels, against a forecast build of around 0.9 million
  • Cushing hub stocks fell about 0.7 million barrels
  • Gasoline was roughly flat versus an expected 1.8 million barrel build, and distillates rose about 1.6 million
  • Strategic Petroleum Reserve holdings fell about 2.9 million barrels as emergency exchange deliveries continue
  • Brent near $89 and WTI around $80 are close to three-month lows on rising supply and surplus concerns
  • Official EIA data is due Wednesday at 15:30 GMT, and OPEC+ meets on Sunday

US crude inventories barely moved last week, according to private data from the American Petroleum Institute (API), coming in well short of expectations for a modest build. The industry survey showed crude stocks up about 0.1 million barrels in the week to 20 November, against a forecast increase of around 0.9 million. Stocks at the Cushing, Oklahoma, delivery hub for US crude futures fell about 0.7 million barrels. Gasoline inventories were roughly flat, compared with expectations for a build of about 1.8 million barrels, while distillate stocks rose about 1.6 million barrels, slightly more than the 1.4 million forecast. The release also showed Strategic Petroleum Reserve holdings down about 2.9 million barrels, as deliveries under the US government's emergency exchange programme continue through November and December.

The numbers land in a market that has shed much of its war premium. Brent crude is trading near $89 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate around $80, both close to three-month lows after a slide of roughly a quarter from late October levels. Reuters reported that prices touched their lowest since late August on Tuesday on signs of rising crude supply and a potential surplus, before steadying as shipping risks in the Strait of Hormuz resurfaced, with three vessels struck by projectiles while transiting the waterway on Monday. The reopening of Libya's Sharara pipeline has added to the supply picture, while US efforts to reach a deal with Iran, with Qatar mediating, have kept traders from rebuilding the risk premium. JPMorgan has argued that once the conflict eases, Middle Eastern producers outside Iran could rush to recover lost market share, adding a wave of supply. OPEC+ meets on Sunday to discuss output, with Brent below the level analysts estimate Saudi Arabia needs to balance its budget.

The API and the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) measure the same thing over the same week, but in different ways. The API, an industry body, compiles figures voluntarily reported by its member companies and publishes them on Tuesday afternoon US time. The EIA, the statistical arm of the Department of Energy, runs a mandatory survey of refiners, terminal operators and pipelines and publishes its Weekly Petroleum Status Report on Wednesday morning. Because coverage and methods differ, the two often disagree, sometimes by several million barrels and occasionally on direction. Traders tend to treat the API as an early read and the EIA as the benchmark, partly because the government report adds production, refinery runs, exports, imports and implied demand.

The official data is due on Wednesday at 15:30 GMT (10:30am US Eastern). A small crude build and a further Cushing draw would offer some support to prices after November's sell-off, though the weekly figures are likely to matter less than the OPEC+ decision and any change in US-Iran talks. Gasoline will be watched closely as US drivers head into the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Copper sends two signals: a 20% slide on the LME, record premiums in China
item.description:
Copper's slide adds to pressure on mining equities and on commodity-linked currencies, including the Australian dollar and the Chilean peso, at a time when wider risk appetite is already fragile. Elevated physical premiums in China give some support beneath prices. If the selling stays in futures and doesn't spread to physical demand, any rebound could be sharp as short positions are closed. Expect volatility to stay high while AI spending headlines drive moves across equities and metals. Copper and oil weakening at the same time may revive talk of a global growth scare, though each market has its own supply story.

---

Copper futures have slumped into bear market territory, but Chinese buyers are paying record premiums for the physical metal, leaving the old growth barometer giving two readings at once.

Summary:

  • LME three-month copper fell back below $12,000 a tonne, about 20% under its September peak
  • Comex copper is also about 20% off its September record, confirming a bear market
  • AI spending doubts, a firmer dollar, higher US rate expectations and trade tension have driven the selling
  • US tariff-driven stockpiles are being shipped back out as the US price premium over London flips to a discount
  • China's Yangshan import premium hit a record, and Shanghai stocks are below one day's consumption
  • Arrivals in China, the US tariff decision and the December Fed meeting are the next tests

Copper's long-standing reputation as a barometer of global growth is being tested, with futures prices and the physical market pointing in different directions. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange fell about 5% on Tuesday to around $11,860 a tonne, Fastmarkets reported. That took it back below $12,000 and roughly 20% under its September peak near $14,900. In New York, Comex copper settled near $5.49 a pound on Friday, also about 20% below its September record, putting both benchmarks in or close to bear market territory. Last week's 9% drop was among the steepest weekly falls of the decade.

The selling has come largely from outside the copper market itself. Doubts about the pace and financing of artificial intelligence spending have hit technology shares. Copper was bid up this year partly on expected data centre demand, and it has traded alongside them. A Monday rebound on Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive was almost fully reversed within a day. A firmer US dollar, the prospect of higher US interest rates, a surprise US midterm election result and reports that Washington was preparing broader tariffs on China and other countries have all weighed on sentiment.

A second force is the unwinding of the US tariff trade. Metal flowed into the United States for much of the past two years ahead of possible duties on refined copper. Broker data now place more than nine in ten tonnes of LME and CME exchange inventory in the US. The US price premium over London has flipped to a discount, and cargoes are being shipped back out, much of it towards China. The proposed tariff has not been formally dropped, but markets have started to trade as though it will not arrive.

The physical picture in China looks very different. The Yangshan import premium, a gauge of what Chinese buyers pay above the exchange price for metal delivered into the country, hit a record of around $500 a tonne last week before easing to about $450. Shanghai warehouse stocks fell to less than a day of Chinese consumption, and the expiring November contract in Shanghai jumped more than 9% on its final trading day to around ¥118,000 a tonne. Some of that tightness reflects a shortage of copper concentrate for smelters rather than stronger buying, which makes it harder to read demand from it.

Views on what the divergence means differ. ING has described the weakness as largely a financial market story rather than a broad deterioration in copper fundamentals. Other analysts have described Monday's rally as short covering rather than a change in sentiment. Some have noted that copper has historically tended to find support around the turn of the year as restocking picks up.

The next few weeks may help settle the question. Copper shipped from the US should start arriving in China, which could ease premiums. How far those premiums fall, and whether exchange prices fall with them or stabilise, will indicate whether the move reflects weaker end demand or a repricing of financial positions. The US tariff decision and the Federal Reserve's December meeting are also likely to matter. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia CPI preview: 4.8% looks like the peak, but the core print will move the RBA
item.description:
The headline rise is largely priced in, so the Australian dollar and short-dated Australian government bond yields are more exposed to the core reading. The Aussie is trading around 66.4 US cents. A trimmed mean of 0.4% or firmer would likely lift front-end yields and support the currency by pushing back expectations for the first rate cut. A 0.3% print would leave in place the banks' expected easing timeline for mid-to-late 2027. US markets are heading into a Thanksgiving-shortened week, so any AUD move may meet thinner liquidity than usual. For energy watchers, the fuel-led headline is another sign of crude prices feeding into inflation and central bank decisions well beyond the US.

Summary:

  • October CPI is due at 00:30 GMT Wednesday (7:30pm US Eastern Tuesday)
  • Headline is expected up 0.4% m/m, taking the annual rate to 4.8% from 4.3%
  • Trimmed mean forecasts split between 0.3% m/m (3.6% y/y) and 0.4% m/m (3.7% y/y)
  • Higher fuel prices and the unwinding of electricity subsidies are the main headline drivers
  • The 1 October ban on card surcharges is an uncertain upside risk to core prices
  • The RBA cash rate is 4.85% after a 6-3 vote to hike in November, and markets see a December hold as near certain

Australia's October consumer price index, due at 00:30 GMT on Wednesday (7:30pm US Eastern on Tuesday), is expected to show headline inflation at what forecasters see as the top of the current cycle. The core reading will shape expectations for when the Reserve Bank of Australia can begin cutting rates. Consensus has headline CPI rising 0.4% over the month, taking the annual rate to 4.8% from 4.3% in September. Forecasts for the trimmed mean, the RBA's preferred core gauge, are less settled. Most calls are at 0.3% m/m with the annual rate holding at 3.6%, while several forecasters see 0.4% and a lift to 3.7%.

The big four banks are split down the middle. Commonwealth Bank and NAB both see headline at 4.7% and the trimmed mean steady at 3.6%. Westpac and ANZ are at 4.8% and 3.7%. In its preview, Westpac forecast monthly gains of around 0.4% for both headline and core and described October as the likely peak in Australian inflation, with the trimmed mean expected to slip below 3% by the third quarter of 2027.

Fuel does most of the work on the headline. NAB estimates higher automotive fuel prices will add around 1.2 points to year-end inflation, and the unwinding of government electricity subsidies adds to the rise. Neither is the kind of domestic demand pressure that monetary policy is designed to lean against. A wildcard sits in the core: card payment surcharges were banned from 1 October, and it is unclear how many businesses folded that cost into their prices. ANZ estimates the change could add about 0.1 point to headline CPI.

The labour market has turned sharply. Unemployment rose to 4.9% in October, its highest since 2021, after a similar upside surprise in September, and the economy shed jobs in both months. At its November meeting the RBA lifted the cash rate to 4.85%, but three of the nine board members preferred to hold, and the statement afterwards no longer flagged further increases.

Markets price a hold at the 7 to 8 December meeting as near certain, and all four major banks expect one. That makes today's numbers a guide to the timing of the first cut, which the banks currently place between June and August 2027. A 0.3% core print would support the view that inflation has peaked and keep mid-2027 easing in sight. A 0.4% or firmer reading would suggest underlying price pressure is fading too slowly for the board to ease soon, even as job losses mount.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The U.S. housing market is in a 'deep freeze' — and the AI boom isn't helping
item.description:
Strip away the AI spending boom and high interest rates are leaving a serious mark on the real economy.

That is the core takeaway from a new Hot Charts note from National Bank of Canada Senior Economist Jocelyn Paquet, who describes the U.S. real estate market as being stuck in a "deep freeze".

It’s not hard to see why. Higher borrowing costs since the pandemic have crushed affordability and pushed would-be buyers to the sidelines. The average U.S. 30-year fixed mortgage rate is sitting in the 7.15% to 7.41% range, about 100 bps above a year ago. Rather than thawing out, the data shows things are actually getting worse:

  • The pending home sales index dropped to the lowest level of transactions in its history in October.

  • Conditions are marginally better, but soft demand has pushed new-home inventory near its highest level since the Great Recession.

  • Permits fell in October to their lowest level since the pandemic.

  • The NAHB Housing Market Index tumbled in November to its lowest reading since 2012.

For homebuilders, the problem isn't just that buyers are sitting on their hands or that financing is expensive. They are also getting squeezed hard on the cost side.

National Bank’s chart on Producer Price Index categories shows that inputs to residential construction have surged nearly 60% since the pandemic began—vastly outpacing headline PPI. When you combine sluggish demand, elevated rates, and a nearly 60% jump in material costs, it’s no wonder the NAHB index is sitting at 14-year lows.

I would also argue that the illegal immigrant crackdown is very likely to be boosting labor costs.

The real story here isn't just housing—it's the two-speed U.S. economy.

"What these data show is that, outside of AI-related sectors, rising interest rates are having a real impact. It is simply being overshadowed by what is one of the biggest investment booms in history," NBF writes.

For traders watching the Fed and the broader growth picture, it’s a good reminder: the interest-rate-sensitive parts of the economy are already hurting. If the AI spending spree ever blinks, there isn't much of a cushion underneath it, at least until the Fed starts cutting.

item.title: Bank of Canada may need to respond sooner or more forcefully to major supply shocks
item.description:
Comments from Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem and highlights from the Bank’s summary of its renewed monetary policy framework crossed the wires.

  • Bank of Canada may need to respond sooner or more forcefully when supply shocks are large, persistent or broad-based.
  • BoC may also need forceful response if demand is strong, or when businesses and households begin to expect higher inflation will persist.
  • Monetary policy decisions should rely on richer evidence, scenario analysis and judgment, rather than on any single model or measure of inflation.
  • Participants in BoC survey indicated they would be willing to tolerate inflation slightly above 2% if it meant people kept jobs and businesses kept running.
  • Deciding in real time whether to look through a shock or respond to it requires a risk management mindset.
  • BoC is therefore investing in models that can better assess supply shocks and capture dynamics of pricing decisions.
  • Monetary policy can temporarily influence housing demand but cannot address supply constraints.
  • Renewed framework drops all mentions of Bank using the 1%–3% target range to seek maximum sustainable employment when conditions warrant.
  • End-year inflation may not be quite as high as the roughly 3.5% the Bank of Canada predicted in October.
  • Businesses are set to pass through more costs to consumers and this second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence.
  • Economy has shown more resilience than we expected.
  • Increased supply shocks mean inflation is likely to be pushed off course more frequently and for longer.
  • Economic shocks are now likely to be larger, more frequent and more difficult to assess in real time. It’s hard to know how monetary policy should respond.
  • A temporary disruption to supply can have bigger, broader and longer-lasting effects on inflation if economy is already running hot.
  • If inflation goes up but is expected to come down on its own, we generally don’t need to respond.
  • If inflation is going to be too high for too long, we would need to hike rates.
  • Monetary policy framework has performed well but that doesn’t mean we can’t do better.
  • We need to communicate more clearly how we use core inflation measures.
  • Our 2% target applies to total CPI inflation. Core measures are an input into our outlook for total CPI, not a target.
  • We will not rely exclusively on the two main core measures.

What it means?

The policy message has a hawkish tilt. Macklem is making clear that the Bank would hike if inflation stayed too high for too long. The economy has been more resilient than expected, and he sees businesses passing more of the oil shock through to consumers. That pass-through is the risk. If it spreads across more prices and households and businesses start expecting higher inflation to stick, the case for a hike gets stronger.

There is a softer point in the near-term outlook. Year-end inflation may come in below the roughly 3.5% the Bank projected in October, and Macklem is willing to look through a rise that unwinds on its own. For traders, the barometer is how broadly those higher costs show up in consumer prices and how long they persist.

As London and European traders head for the exits, the major indices are lower. Italy’s FTSE MIB leads the way down with a -1.84% decline, followed by Germany's Dax at -1.26%.  Spain’s IBEX 35 fell -0.86%, while France’s CAC 40 and the UK’s FTSE 100 are holding up better.

  • German Dax, 25017.82, down -1.26%
  • France’s CAC 40, 8,040.50, down 0.05%
  • UK’s FTSE 100, 10,467.08, down 0.13%
  • Spain’s IBEX 35, 19,015.81, down 0.86%
  • Italy’s FTSE MIB, 48,121.18, down 1.84%

Tariffs take over from Nvidia

Yesterday it was the return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO that got the buyers going. The Nasdaq 100 gained 6.86% on the day. Today, the focus is back on tariffs. The Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration is preparing new levies on China, the EU and 14 other economies following an investigation into industrial subsidies. The findings could come as early as this week. The detail that caught the market’s attention was the breadth of the plan. The levies could cover a wide range of imports and rise further if trading partners leave their industrial policies in place. That puts the risk of stickier inflation back in focus with the Fed already in a hiking cycle. investinglive.com

In the U.S., the S&P 500 was down about 1.1% and the Nasdaq Composite was down 2.1% in the late morning. Monday’s rally was impressive, but the broader indices fell short of the upside levels that would have shifted more of the bias back to the buyers. Today’s move lower keeps the sellers in control for now. investinglive.com

European yields split. The U.S. curve flattens.

Germany’s 10-year yield fell 1.0 basis point to 3.267%, the UK’s slipped 0.7 basis points to 5.198%, and France was essentially unchanged at 4.785%. Spain’s yield rose 0.8 basis points to 3.876%, while Italy’s rose 2.6 basis points to 4.370%. That widened the Italy–Germany spread by 3.6 basis points to just over 110 basis points, alongside Italy’s underperformance in equities.

In the U.S., the 2-year yield was up 0.7 basis points to 4.673%, while the 5-year was down 2.0 basis points to 4.710%, the 10-year was down 2.2 basis points to 4.898%, and the 30-year was down 1.2 basis points to 5.283%.

The data were stronger on both sides of the Atlantic

Germany’s Ifo business climate index rose to 90.6 from a revised 90.1, just above the 90.5 estimate. Both current conditions and expectations improved. Services and trade did better, while manufacturing sentiment slipped after six consecutive increases. investinglive.com

In the U.S., consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 versus 92.5 expected and 91.9 last month. Both the present situation and expectations improved. investinglive.com  The Richmond Fed manufacturing index also beat expectations, rising to +3 from −2 versus a −3 forecast. New orders led the improvement, moving to +2 from −8, while shipments and employment also picked up. Input costs grew faster, while selling-price growth held steady. investinglive.com

The Swiss franc leads. Silver takes the biggest hit.

The dollar was lower against most of the majors, with the biggest move against the Swiss franc. USDCHF fell 0.71% to 0.8355 after trading as low as 0.8345. EURUSD rose 0.57% to 1.0963 and GBPUSD gained 0.56% to 1.3104. NZDUSD rose 0.51% to 0.5477, AUDUSD edged up 0.09% to 0.6632, and USDCAD fell 0.30% to 1.4316. The yen was the exception, with USDJPY up 0.16% to 159.25.

The softer dollar and lower long-end Treasury yields offered little support to metals. Gold fell 1.81% to $3,569.05, silver dropped 5.13% to $40.93, and copper fell 5.47% to $5.3260. WTI went the other way, rising 0.64% to $80.68 after trading between $79.07 and $81.65.

Bitcoin was down 2.77% at $59,512, back below $60,000. investinglive.com The better barometer for the short-term bias is still the old floor at $61,183–$62,470. Stay below that area and the sellers have the edge, with $58,000 and Friday’s low at $55,081 the next downside levels to watch.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCHF breaks below both hourly moving averages. Sellers eye 0.8339–0.8348.
item.description:
The USDCHF has moved sharply lower after running into a ceiling near 0.8443 over the last four or so trading days. The buyers had several chances to extend the November rally through that level. Each time they fell short. Today, the sellers took the next step, pushing the price below the 100-hour moving average at 0.84143 and then the 200-hour moving average at 0.83992.

The pair is now trading near 0.8355, with the next test just below. A downward-sloping trend line meets a swing area between 0.8339 and 0.8348. That swing area has a number of reactions going back to October and again in November. With the price approaching it after a sharp move lower, it’s a place where buyers can lean against support and define their risk.

What would give the sellers more confidence? A move below 0.8339 that can stay below would open the door toward 0.83224, the 38.2% retracement of the November rally. Below that, 0.83121 is the next downside target. Get through that level and the 50% midpoint at 0.82851 comes into focus.

If the swing area holds and the price bounces, 0.83806 is the first upside hurdle. The 200-hour moving average at 0.83992 is the bigger barometer. As long as the price stays below it, the sellers keep the advantage. A move back above it would give buyers room to target the 100-hour moving average at 0.84143.

Fundamentally,  SNB Vice Chairman Antoine Martin said over the weekend that inflation has accelerated since the central bank’s September meeting and that policymakers are watching for signs that higher costs are feeding into broader prices. Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October from 1.0% in September, more than expected. With the SNB’s policy rate still at 0%, that has put a possible December hike on traders’ radar. Those comments were already out heading into today’s session, but they give traders a reason to favor the franc as the Nvidia-led rally fades and demand for safe havens picks up.

The trading lesson

The ceiling at 0.8443 showed where the buyers were having trouble. The breaks below the hourly moving averages showed that sellers were starting to take control. Now the question is whether they can keep that control through support. If the price breaks below 0.8339 and then stalls on a bounce back into the swing area, sellers have a level to lean against with close risk. If the price quickly gets back above 0.8348, that would be an early warning that the break is failing.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Stock markets fall as Trump pivots from corporate meddling to fresh tariffs
item.description:
The duality of Trump has been on full display this week.

Yesterday, he helped stock markets by intervening to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Today, he's preparing to announce new tariffs on China and dozens of other countries and that's weighing on markets.

The S&P 500 is down 1.1% and the Nasdaq lower by 2.1%.

The WSJ was earlier out with the scoop, and it says that the US will hit China, the EU and many other countries with tariffs due to industrial subsidies. That said, it's not a surprise, the Trump administration has been working to reconstruct its tariff regime on firmer legal grounds since the Supreme Court struck down its original tariffs in February. Notably, on Friday Jamieson Greer told Bloomberg that the subsidy investigation would be done very soon and certainly before year end. There has been talk since August that the US was looking to add an additional 7.5% tariff on China.

These levels wouldn't be a surprise as they would return to the status quo from 2025.

The surpris is that the administration intends to target most imports rather than only industrial sectors with demonstrable excess capacity and it has provisions for tariffs to rise further if foreign countries don't change industrial policies.

Now this isn't another Liberation Day but it's an inflationary move into a time when the Fed is already hiking. The market is priced for 26 bps in December and 58 bps through March. That's come in since the latest market volatility but this threatens to make inflation more sticky and hit consumers with tariff headlines just as they're getting ready to go Christmas shopping.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US broader stock indices give up some of the gains from yesterday with sellers remaining in control
item.description:
Yesterday’s rally was impressive. The major US stock indices had their best day since April 2025, rebounding sharply from Friday’s lows. But after last week’s selloff, the buyers had a lot of ground to make up. All three broader indices fell short of the resistance levels they needed to break to shift the technical bias in their favor.

Today, the indices are giving back some of those gains. That keeps the sellers in control for now. The levels that capped yesterday’s rebound are still the barometers for the next move. If the buyers can get above those levels and stay above them, they can start to take back control. If the rally stalls below resistance again, the focus turns back to support and how much of yesterday’s bounce the buyers can defend.

A brief look at the technicals for the S&P, Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 indices. 

S&P: Yesterday, tThe S&P index moved above a swing area target and broken 38.2% retracement near 7237 and 7260. The high price fell short of another swing area near 7300 and 7321. The 200 day moving average at 7351.20 is also above and was not tested during yesterday's run to the upside. The price is now down below those levels and looking back toward the 50% midpoint that 7079.50.

Nasdaq composite: The NASDAQ composite rose to a old floor area between 24206 and 24425 during yesterday's trade but backed off into the close. Today the price is moving lower and looks toward the 61.8% retracement at 23376.66.

Nasdaq 100: The NASDAQ 100 rallied up toward the 50% midpoint of the move up from the end of March low to the high price reached in October at 27101, but fell short of that target yesterday. The move lower today is now testing the 61.8% retracement of the same move to the upside at 26096. Move below is more bearish.

In the video above, I take a closer look at the S&P 500, the Nasdaq Composite and the Nasdaq 100. I outline the levels buyers need to break to shift the bias, where they can lean against support to keep risk close, and the downside targets that come into play if that support gives way.

item.title: Richmond Fed composite Index for November comes in higher at 3 versus -2 last month
item.description:
The Richmond Fed composite Index for the month of November comes in stronger at 3 versus -2 last month.

  • Richmond Fed manufacturing index — +3 vs −2 forecast. Prior −2.

November components vs October

  • New orders — +2 vs −8
  • Shipments — +2 vs 0
  • Employment — +6 vs +3
  • Local business conditions — +4 vs −8
  • Prices paid, 12-month growth — 7.59% vs 7.12%
  • Prices received, 12-month growth — 5.27% vs 5.27%

Fifth District manufacturing activity improved modestly in November, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond. The composite index moved back above zero after two months at −2. New orders led the rebound, while shipments and employment also improved.

The outlook firmed as well. Expected shipments rose to 28 from 19, expected new orders to 27 from 22, and expected employment to 13 from 8. Input costs grew faster, while selling-price growth held steady. Firms expect both rates to ease over the next 12 months.

The current condition components for November vs October sees MoM improvement, but inflation rises

  • Manufacturing index: +3 vs −2, up 5 points
  • Shipments: +2 vs 0, up 2 points
  • New orders: +2 vs −8, up 10 points
  • Order backlogs: −6 vs −21, up 15 points
  • Capacity utilization: 0 vs −7, up 7 points
  • Vendor lead times: +16 vs +18, down 2 points
  • Local business conditions: +4 vs −8, up 12 points
  • Capital expenditures: −10 vs −12, up 2 points
  • Finished goods inventories: +4 vs +4, unchanged
  • Raw materials inventories: 0 vs −2, up 2 points
  • Equipment and software spending: −9 vs −8, down 1 point
  • Services expenditures: −5 vs −19, up 14 points
  • Employment: +6 vs +3, up 3 points
  • Wages: +24 vs +20, up 4 points
  • Availability of needed skills: −10 vs −7, down 3 points
  • Prices paid growth: 7.59% vs 7.12%, up 0.47 percentage points
  • Prices received growth: 5.27% vs 5.27%, unchanged

Current conditions improved across most of the Richmond Fed’s November manufacturing survey. Of the 17 current readings, including the headline index, 12 rose, three fell and two were unchanged. The composite index rose 5 points to +3 from −2, with all three of its components improving. New orders led the way, rising 10 points to +2, while employment rose 3 points and shipments rose 2 points. Order backlogs posted the biggest gain, up 15 points, though they remained negative at −6. Services spending rose 14 points but also stayed negative, while local business conditions climbed 12 points to +4.

The weaker spots were equipment and software spending, which slipped 1 point to −9, and the availability of needed skills, which fell 3 points to −10. Vendor lead times accounted for the third decline, though the lower reading signals that delivery times lengthened less broadly. On prices, input-cost growth picked up to 7.59% from 7.12%, while selling-price growth held at 5.27%. Finished goods inventories were also unchanged.

The Expectation components also shows improvement with lower inflation expectations. 

  • Shipments: +28 vs +19, up 9 points
  • New orders: +27 vs +22, up 5 points
  • Order backlogs: +7 vs +7, unchanged
  • Capacity utilization: +10 vs +8, up 2 points
  • Vendor lead times: +14 vs +13, up 1 point
  • Local business conditions: +15 vs +7, up 8 points
  • Capital expenditures: −1 vs +4, down 5 points
  • Finished goods inventories: −3 vs +3, down 6 points
  • Raw materials inventories: −3 vs −3, unchanged
  • Equipment and software spending: +3 vs +2, up 1 point
  • Services expenditures: −9 vs −12, up 3 points
  • Employment: +13 vs +8, up 5 points
  • Wages: +44 vs +49, down 5 points
  • Availability of needed skills: −6 vs −7, up 1 point
  • Expected prices paid growth: 5.06% vs 5.32%, down 0.26 percentage points
  • Expected prices received growth: 3.82% vs 4.30%, down 0.48 percentage points

Expectations improved across much of the Richmond Fed’s November manufacturing survey. Of the 16 forward-looking readings, nine rose, five fell and two were unchanged. Expected shipments posted the biggest gain, rising 9 points to +28, while expected local business conditions climbed 8 points to +15. The outlook for new orders and employment also firmed, with both indexes up 5 points to +27 and +13, respectively. The expected availability of needed skills improved by 1 point but remained negative at −6.

Capital spending was the clearest weak spot, with the expectations index falling 5 points to −1 from +4 despite the stronger outlook for orders and shipments. Expected finished goods inventories fell 6 points to −3, and the wages index eased 5 points to +44. Firms also lowered their 12-month growth expectations for both prices paid, to 5.06% from 5.32%, and prices received, to 3.82% from 4.30%. Expectations for order backlogs and raw materials inventories were unchanged. The inflation guidance is good news. 

Quick analysis

The move back above zero is a modest positive for manufacturing, with new orders the component to watch for follow-through. Firmer demand and faster input-cost growth could lend some support to the US dollar and Treasury yields. Steady selling-price growth and expectations for easing price pressures limit what one regional survey is likely to change for the Fed.

What this report measures

The Richmond Fed’s monthly survey tracks shipments, new orders and employment at manufacturers in the Fifth Federal Reserve District. The seasonally adjusted composite is a diffusion index. A positive reading means improvement was more widespread than deterioration, and traders use it as an early regional read on factory demand and hiring.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US November consumer confidence 103.3 vs 92.5 expected
item.description:
• Prior was 91.7 (revised to 91.9)
  • Present situation 132.8 vs 120.4 prior
  • Expectations 83.6 vs 72.6 prior
  • The share of consumers saying jobs are “plentiful” minus the share saying jobs are “hard to get”—improved by 7.6 ppts to +12.4%.

This is a great rebound in a beaten-down series but likely reflects the politics that have infected everything and the passing of the midterms. Two months ago, the series was at the lowest since 2014. That said, last week's major retailer earnings and commentary was positive on the macro side.

Today, retail comps came in solid. Best Buy led at +6.1%, its best in five years and nearly triple the 2.3% consensus. Abercrombie was next at +6%, with every region accelerating, then Dollar Tree at +4.6% on 3.8% traffic growth and Kohl's at +1.2%, its first top-line growth in more than four years.

The macro read is less clean. Best Buy's blended ASPs rose 6% with units flat, and computing prices jumped 25% on memory costs while units fell mid-teens. That's goods inflation flattering nominal sales, and HPE says memory supply stays tight into H2 2028. Dollar Tree's traffic points to continued trade-down. Tariff refunds flattered margins everywhere and Dollar Tree is putting some of that money into lower prices, but none of it repeats in Q4. Best Buy's 2-4% Q4 comp guide says the pace is already cooling.

“Consumer confidence rallied again in November, potentially due to lower uncertainty following the midterm elections,” said Fergus McCormick, Senior Economist, Global Indicators, The Conference Board. “After two months of consecutive increases, the headline index is back to levels of confidence last seen in January 2025. The gain in confidence was led by stronger perceptions of present and future labor market conditions. Perceptions of current and future business conditions also improved sharply. Along with the gain in headline confidence, consumers planned slightly higher spending on goods and vacations.”

For background, the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index is released at 10 am ET on the last Tuesday of each month, making it the final major read on US household sentiment before the month closes. It's benchmarked to 100 in 1985 and is one of two headline sentiment gauges, alongside the University of Michigan survey.

The index combines consumers' views on current conditions with their outlook for the next six months. The Present Situation Index reflects how people assess business conditions and the job market today. The Expectations Index captures their outlook for business conditions, employment and household income six months ahead. The Conference Board has long noted that an Expectations Index below 80 has historically signaled a recession within the following year.

Its biggest distinction from the Michigan survey is a heavier focus on jobs. The most closely watched detail is the labor differential, the share of respondents who say jobs are "plentiful" minus the share who say jobs are "hard to get." It tracks the unemployment rate closely and often turns before the official labor data, which makes it a useful cross-check ahead of the monthly payrolls report.

The survey also covers 12-month inflation expectations, expectations for interest rates and stock prices, and plans to buy homes, vehicles and big-ticket appliances. Open-ended responses show what's weighing on consumers, whether prices, tariffs, politics or job security.

Confidence measures have a loose relationship with actual spending, and consumers frequently keep spending even when they report feeling gloomy. Markets usually react only to large surprises. The report's main value is in its labor market detail and in tracking how households are responding to inflation, gasoline prices and the jobs picture heading into the holiday shopping season.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.
